questions.stem: Which one of the following protocols may need to broadcast some of its messages?

steps.title: What broadcast means and the rule
steps.body: A broadcast is a message sent to every host on the local network at once, using the all-ones address 255.255.255.255 as the destination. A host broadcasts only when it does not know who to talk to. The rule: a protocol broadcasts when it must find a server before it has any address to use.

steps.title: Who has no address
steps.body: SMTP (mail), FTP (files) and HTTP (web) are all started by a client that already has an IP address and already knows the server name or address. They open a TCP connection to one named server. TCP connections are one-to-one, so they can never be broadcast.

steps.title: DHCP is the exception
steps.body: A machine that has just joined the network has no IP address and does not know where the DHCP server is. It sends DHCPDISCOVER to 255.255.255.255 so that any server on the link can hear it. That is a broadcast, so the answer is DHCP, option (C).

shortcut.body: Ask which protocol runs before the host has an address. Only DHCP does, so it must broadcast. About 15 seconds.

traps.text: SMTP sends mail over a TCP connection to one named mail server; TCP has no broadcast.
FTP opens TCP connections to one server, so it never broadcasts.
HTTP is a TCP request to one web server; the client already knows the server address from DNS.

recognize.clues: The words "may need to broadcast some of its messages" point to a protocol that runs before the host is configured, which is the job of an IP support protocol rather than an application protocol.
recognize.contrast: ARP also broadcasts, but it is not offered here and it resolves a known IP to a hardware address; the protocol asked for here hands out the IP address itself.

check.body: Take the destination 255.255.255.255 and ask what each transport allows. A TCP endpoint is one unicast IP address plus a port, so a TCP segment cannot be addressed to the broadcast address, which rules out SMTP, FTP and HTTP. DHCP uses UDP ports 67 (server) and 68 (client), and a UDP datagram may be sent to a broadcast address.

hints.text: Ask what a host must already know before it can start talking to a server. Which of the four protocols could be running at a moment when the host knows nothing yet?
A broadcast goes to every host on the local link at once. A TCP connection, by contrast, is a conversation between exactly two endpoints.
A protocol needs a broadcast only when it must locate a peer without knowing any address for it. If the peer address is already known, a direct message does the job.
For each protocol, note whether it rides on TCP and whether the client already has a source address and a server address when it begins. Rule out those that do.

variation.stem: A host on a LAN knows the IP address of another host on the same LAN but not its hardware (MAC) address. Which protocol sends a broadcast frame to find it?
variation.explanation: The sender needs a MAC address to build the frame, and it has none for that IP, so it asks everyone on the link. ARP does this with a broadcast request that only the owner of the IP answers. DNS, SMTP and FTP all assume the link-layer address is already resolved and send to one named server.

questions.stem: If an IP network uses a subnet mask of 255.255.240.0, the maximum number of IP addresses that can be assigned to network interfaces is __________. (answer in integer)

steps.title: Terms and rule
steps.body: A subnet mask is 32 bits: ones mark the network part, zeros mark the host part. If $h$ bits are zeros, the network holds $2^h$ addresses. The first (all host bits 0) is the network address and the last (all host bits 1) is the broadcast address; neither can be given to an interface. So usable addresses are $2^h-2$.

steps.title: Count the zero bits
steps.body: 255.255.240.0 in binary is 11111111.11111111.11110000.00000000. The third octet 240 is 11110000, which has 4 zeros, and the fourth octet has 8 zeros. So $h = 4+8 = 12$ and the prefix is /20.

steps.title: Compute
steps.body: Usable interface addresses are $2^{12}-2 = 4096-2 = 4094$.

shortcut.body: Mask 240 in the third octet means 4 host bits there, plus 8 in the last octet gives 12 bits, so $2^{12}-2 = 4094$. 20 seconds.

traps.text: 4096 forgets that the network and broadcast addresses cannot be assigned.

recognize.clues: A dotted-decimal mask 255.255.240.0 is given and the question asks for the number of addressable interfaces, so the work is converting the mask to host bits and counting usable hosts.
recognize.contrast: A CIDR question hands you the prefix length (such as /20) and asks the same host count. Here the mask is dotted-decimal, so first turn it into a prefix or count its zero bits; the arithmetic after that is identical, including subtracting the network and broadcast addresses.

check.body: Use the block size in the third octet instead: 256 - 240 = 16 consecutive third-octet values, each with 256 fourth-octet values, so the block spans 16 x 256 = 4096 addresses. The prefix check agrees: 20 network bits plus 12 host bits make 32. Two of the 4096 are reserved.

hints.text: Which bits of the mask are ones and which are zeros? The zeros tell you how many addresses the block holds.
The mask splits a 32-bit address into a network part and a host part. The number of zero bits in the mask is the number of host bits.
With $h$ host bits a block holds $2^h$ addresses, but the all-zeros host (network address) and all-ones host (broadcast address) cannot go to an interface.
Write the third octet 240 in binary and count its zero bits, then add the 8 zero bits of the fourth octet to get $h$.
Octet 240 is 11110000, so it contributes 4 zero bits. Add the zeros of the last octet yourself.

variation.stem: If an IP network uses a subnet mask of 255.255.248.0, the maximum number of IP addresses that can be assigned to network interfaces is ________. (answer in integer)
variation.explanation: 248 is 11111000, so the third octet has 3 zero bits; adding the 8 zero bits of the last octet gives 11 host bits. The block holds $2^{11}=2048$ addresses, and removing the network and broadcast addresses leaves 2046.

questions.stem: An ISP having an address block 202.16.0.0/15 assigns a block of 6000 IP addresses to a client, using the classless internet domain routing (CIDR) super-netting approach. Which of the following address blocks can be assigned by the ISP?

solutionDiagram.alt: Third octets of 202.16.0.0/15 drawn as /19 cells of 32; three options fill whole cells, 202.17.24.0/19 straddles two cells.

steps.title: Terms and rules
steps.body: CIDR hands out blocks of $2^k$ addresses written as address/prefix, where prefix = $32-k$. Two rules decide whether a block is valid. Size: it must hold at least the number of addresses asked for. Alignment: its first address must be a multiple of its size, i.e. all host bits of the start address are 0. It must also lie inside the ISP block.

steps.title: Size
steps.body: 6000 addresses need $2^k\ge 6000$. $2^{12}=4096$ is too small and $2^{13}=8192$ is enough, so $k=13$ and the prefix is /19. All four options are /19, so size is not what separates them.

steps.title: The ISP block
steps.body: 202.16.0.0/15 has 17 host bits, so it spans 202.16.0.0 to 202.17.255.255: third octet from 0 to 255 under both 202.16 and 202.17. A /19 block spans 32 values of the third octet, so it must start at a third octet that is a multiple of 32.

steps.title: Check each option
steps.body: (A) 202.16.0.0: third octet 0 is a multiple of 32, inside the ISP block, valid. (B) 202.17.64.0: 64 is a multiple of 32, inside, valid. (C) 202.16.32.0: 32 is a multiple of 32, valid. (D) 202.17.24.0: 24 is not a multiple of 32, so the start address has host bits set; the true /19 containing it is 202.17.0.0/19. Not a valid block. Answer: A, B and C.

shortcut.body: Prefix is /19 since $2^{13}=8192\ge6000$. Then test the third octet of each start address: it must be a multiple of 32. 0, 64 and 32 pass; 24 fails. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Choosing only one option: the question asks which blocks can be assigned and three are valid, so select all.
Using /20 (4096 addresses) because 6000 is close to 4096; it is too small for 6000 hosts.
Accepting 202.17.24.0/19 because it looks like a /19 and lies in the range; its start is not on a 32 boundary.

recognize.clues: An ISP block in /15 notation, a request for a number of addresses, and a list of address/prefix blocks to choose from signal CIDR allocation: size the block, then test alignment and containment.
recognize.contrast: Route aggregation asks which prefix covers several routes; here a single client block is carved out of a larger one, so the question is alignment, not summarisation.

check.body: Convert the third octet to a plain offset: a /19 block must start at an address that is a multiple of 8192 within the 2^16-address space of the third and fourth octets. Third octet 0, 32 and 64 give offsets 0, 8192 and 16384, all multiples of 8192. Third octet 24 gives 6144, which is not.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: GATE CSE 2026 Set 1 question 56
GATE 2026 CS-1 answer key, IIT Guwahati (organising institute)

hints.text: Two separate conditions must hold for a block to be assignable. What are they, and does each option meet both?
A CIDR block of $2^k$ addresses is written address/prefix. Its first address must have all host bits equal to zero, and the block must fit inside the ISP block.
The size must reach 6000 addresses, so find the smallest power of two that does. A block with that many addresses must start at a multiple of its own size.
Find the prefix length from the size, work out how many third-octet values one block spans, and then test whether each option third octet is a multiple of that span.
$2^{13}=8192$ is the smallest power of two above 6000, so every option is a /19 and one block spans 32 values of the third octet.

variation.stem: An ISP holds the block 172.16.0.0/14 and must assign a block for a client that needs 3000 addresses using CIDR. Which of the following blocks can be assigned? (select all that apply)
variation.explanation: 3000 addresses need $2^{12}=4096$, so the prefix is /20 and a block spans 16 values of the third octet. 172.17.32.0 and 172.19.240.0 start on multiples of 16 and lie inside 172.16.0.0 to 172.19.255.255. 172.18.8.0 starts at 8, which is not a multiple of 16, and 172.20.0.0 is outside the ISP block.

questions.stem:
Consider the routing protocols given in List I and the names given in List II:
(i) Distance vector routing  (a) Bellman-Ford
(ii) Link state routing  (b) Dijkstra
For matching of items in List I with those in List II, which ONE of the following options is CORRECT?

steps.title: Two ways to compute shortest paths
steps.body: Distance vector (DV) routing: each router tells only its neighbours its table of distances, and updates its own table with $d(x,y)=\min_v\,[c(x,v)+d(v,y)]$ over its neighbours $v$. This repeated relaxation is the Bellman-Ford equation. Link state (LS) routing: every router floods the cost of its own links to everyone, so each router holds the whole map and then runs Dijkstra on it.

steps.title: Match
steps.body: (i) distance vector uses the Bellman-Ford equation, so (i)-(a). (ii) link state runs Dijkstra on the full map, so (ii)-(b). That is option (A).

shortcut.body: DV = neighbours only = Bellman-Ford; LS = full map = Dijkstra. 10 seconds.

traps.text: Both to Bellman-Ford confuses the map each router holds in LS with the relaxation DV uses.
The reverse matching: DV never has the whole graph, so Dijkstra cannot run there.
Both to Dijkstra: only LS has the full topology Dijkstra needs.

recognize.clues: The two lists pair routing families with named algorithms, so the question is which algorithm each family runs, decided by what each router knows.
recognize.contrast: Both families compute shortest paths, so they look alike; tell them apart by knowledge: neighbours only (distance vector) versus the full flooded map (link state).

check.body: Test the pairing by feasibility. A distance vector router has only its neighbour costs and the vectors they send, so it could not run Dijkstra, which needs every edge of the graph. A link state router already has every edge, so it has no reason to rely on neighbour estimates. Only one pairing is feasible for both.

GATE 2025 CS-2 final answer key, IIT Roorkee (organising institute)

hints.text: For each routing style, ask what information a router holds: only its neighbours, or the whole network map?
In distance vector routing a router shares its table of distances with its neighbours and improves its own table from what they report.
Dijkstra needs every link cost of the graph before it can start. An update rule of the form minimum over neighbours of cost plus neighbour distance is a different algorithm.
Match each name in List II to the routing style whose knowledge it can actually use, then compare the pairings in the four options.

variation.stem: Which one of the following statements about routing is correct?
options: In link state routing each router sends its whole routing table only to its neighbours
In distance vector routing each router floods the costs of all links to every router
In link state routing each router floods the costs of its own links and runs Dijkstra on the full map
In distance vector routing each router holds the full network map and runs Dijkstra
variation.explanation: Link state routers flood the costs of their own links so every router builds the same map, then run Dijkstra. Distance vector routers exchange distance tables with neighbours only and apply the Bellman-Ford update. The other three statements swap these two behaviours.

questions.stem:
A machine receives an IPv4 datagram. The protocol field of the IPv4 header has the protocol number of a protocol X.
Which ONE of the following is NOT a possible candidate for X?

steps.title: What the protocol field is
steps.body: The IPv4 header has an 8-bit protocol field naming the protocol of the data inside the packet, so the receiver can hand it to the right module: 6 for TCP, 17 for UDP, and so on. The rule: a protocol can appear there only if it is carried directly in an IP packet, with no TCP or UDP header in between.

steps.title: Check each protocol
steps.body: ICMP is carried directly in IP (number 1). IGMP is carried directly in IP (number 2). OSPF is carried directly in IP (number 89). RIP is different: it sends its messages inside UDP datagrams to UDP port 520, so the IP protocol field of a RIP packet says 17 (UDP), never a RIP number.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: RIP cannot be X, option (D).

shortcut.body: Remember: OSPF goes straight over IP (89); RIP rides on UDP (port 520), BGP on TCP (port 179). 15 seconds.

traps.text: ICMP does have its own protocol number (1), so it is a candidate and not the answer.
IGMP has protocol number 2.
OSPF is easy to guess as application-level like RIP, but it runs directly over IP with number 89.

recognize.clues: The stem mentions the protocol field of the IPv4 header and asks which protocol cannot be its value, so the test is whether the protocol is carried directly over IP.
recognize.contrast: Do not confuse a routing protocol that runs over IP directly with one that is an application over UDP or TCP; both are called routing protocols but differ in what the IP protocol field holds.

check.body: A second route is the port test. A protocol that is assigned a port number has a UDP or TCP header between it and IP, so the IP field shows 17 or 6, never its own number. Exactly one of the four options has a well-known port, and the other three have no port at all.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: GATE CSE 2025 Set 2 question 18
GATE 2025 CS-2 final answer key, IIT Roorkee (organising institute)

hints.text: The question is about what sits directly inside an IP packet. Which of these four protocols are not placed there directly?
The protocol field in the IPv4 header names the next-level protocol that the payload belongs to, such as TCP or UDP.
A protocol can fill that field only if its messages are carried straight in IP. A protocol carried inside a UDP or TCP segment shows the transport protocol in that field instead.
For each of the four protocols, recall whether it uses a transport port. Protocols that use a port live above the transport layer.

variation.stem: Which ONE of the following protocols has its messages placed directly inside an IPv4 packet, so that it has its own number in the IPv4 protocol field?
variation.explanation: OSPF is carried straight in IP with protocol number 89. RIP and DNS ride on UDP (ports 520 and 53) and BGP rides on TCP port 179, so an IP packet carrying them shows 17 or 6 in the protocol field.

questions.stem:
Consider a network that uses Ethernet and IPv4. Assume that IPv4 headers do not use any options field. Each Ethernet frame can carry a maximum of 1500 bytes in its data field. A UDP segment is transmitted. The payload (data) in the UDP segment is 7488 bytes.
Which ONE of the following choices has the CORRECT total number of fragments transmitted and the size of the last fragment including IPv4 header?

solutionDiagram.alt: Bar of 7496 IP data bytes cut into five fragments of 1480 data bytes and a last fragment of 96 data bytes.

steps.title: Terms and rule
steps.body: The MTU (maximum transmission unit) is the largest IP packet a link carries: here 1500 bytes, header included. When a datagram is bigger, it is cut into fragments. Each fragment has its own 20-byte header (no options), and its data length must be a multiple of 8 bytes except in the last fragment, because the offset field counts in 8-byte units.

steps.title: Size of the IP data
steps.body: The UDP segment is the data of the IP datagram. It is an 8-byte UDP header plus the 7488-byte payload: $7488+8=7496$ bytes. The 7488 given is the UDP payload, so the header must be added.

steps.title: Data per fragment
steps.body: Each frame carries 1500 bytes, of which 20 are IP header, leaving 1480 for data. 1480 is a multiple of 8 (185 units), so full fragments carry 1480.

steps.title: Count and last size
steps.body: $7496/1480 = 5.06$, so 5 full fragments carry 7400 bytes and a sixth carries $7496-7400=96$ data bytes. With its header it is $96+20=116$ bytes. 6 fragments, 116 bytes: option (D).

shortcut.body: Add the 8-byte UDP header: 7496. Divide by 1480: 5 full plus 96 left, so 6 fragments and 96+20 = 116. If you forget the UDP header you get 88 or 108 and fall for options (B)/(C). 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: 5 fragments: treats 7488 as nearly 5 x 1500 and ignores that each fragment loses 20 bytes to its header.
88 bytes: forgets the UDP header (7488 - 7400 = 88) and also forgets to add the IP header back.
108 bytes: forgets the 8-byte UDP header, 88 data bytes + 20 header.

recognize.clues: An MTU of 1500, a no-options IPv4 header, and a UDP payload larger than one frame call for fragmentation: count fragments and size the leftover piece with its header.
recognize.contrast: Do not treat the 7488 bytes as the IP data directly; a UDP payload gets the 8-byte UDP header first, unlike a question that gives the IP datagram size itself.

check.body: Reassemble. Five fragments of 1480 plus one of 96 data bytes sum to 7400 + 96 = 7496, the UDP segment size, so nothing is lost or counted twice. The last fragment starts at offset 7400/8 = 925, well inside the 13-bit offset field. On the wire the headers add 6 x 20 = 120 bytes.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: GATE CSE 2025 Set 2 question 23
GATE 2025 CS-2 final answer key, IIT Roorkee (organising institute)

hints.text: Is the 7488 the size of the packet that IP will fragment? Think about which headers are added before IP cuts anything.
The MTU limits the whole IP packet, header included, and every fragment carries its own IP header.
Fragment offsets count in units of 8 bytes, so every fragment except the last must carry a multiple of 8 data bytes.
Add the transport header to the payload to get the IP data, find the data capacity of one fragment after removing the IP header, and divide.
One fragment carries 1500 minus 20 header bytes, which is 1480 data bytes, and 1480 is already a multiple of 8.

variation.stem: A network uses Ethernet and IPv4 with no header options, and each frame carries at most 1500 bytes of data. A UDP segment with a 5000-byte payload is sent. Which choice gives the correct number of IP fragments and the size of the last fragment including its IPv4 header?
variation.explanation: The UDP segment is 5000 + 8 = 5008 bytes. Each fragment holds 1480 data bytes, so 3 full fragments take 4440 and the last holds 568 bytes, 588 with its header. That is 4 fragments. Dropping the UDP header gives 580; counting only full fragments gives 3.

questions.stem: A packet with the destination IP address 145.36.109.70 arrives at a router whose routing table is shown. Which interface will the packet be forwarded to?

solutionDiagram.alt: Number line of the third octet 0 to 255 with the /16, /17 and /18 blocks as bars and a marker at 109 inside the /16 and /18 bars only.

steps.title: Rule: longest prefix match
steps.body: A router table entry is a prefix: the first $N$ bits of an address, written /N. An address matches an entry when its first $N$ bits equal the prefix. Several entries can match; the router must pick the one with the largest $N$ (the most specific), because a longer prefix describes a smaller, more exact group of addresses. The default route matches everything and is used only when nothing else does.

steps.title: Match by octets
steps.body: The destination is 145.36.109.70. The first two octets 145.36 are fixed by /16, so they decide /16 entries alone. The third octet 109 is 01101101 in binary. For /17 the first bit of the third octet must equal the prefix: 145.36.128.0 has third octet 10000000, its first bit is 1, but 109 starts with 0, so /17 fails. For /18 the first two bits of the third octet must match: 145.36.64.0 has 01000000, first two bits 01, and 109 starts with 01, so /18 matches.

steps.title: Pick the longest
steps.body: /16 matches (E1), /18 matches (E3), /17 does not, /24 145.36.255.0 does not (third octet 255 is not 109), default is only a fallback. Longest of /16 and /18 is /18, so E3, option (A).

shortcut.body: Third octet 109 lies in 64 to 127, which is the /18 block 145.36.64.0 (a /18 spans 64 values). Longest match wins. 1 minute.

traps.text: E1 is the /16, which matches too, but it is shorter than the /18 that also matches.
E2 is the /17 starting at 128; the third octet 109 is below 128 so it is not in it.
E5 is the default; used only when no listed prefix matches.

recognize.clues: A routing table of nested prefixes of different lengths plus a default route, and a single destination address, call for longest prefix match.
recognize.contrast: This is not subnet counting or CIDR allocation: nothing is being sized or assigned, a destination is only looked up against overlapping prefixes.

check.body: Use integer ranges. Third octet times 256 plus the last octet gives 109 x 256 + 70 = 27974 within the 16-bit tail. The /17 at 128 starts at 32768, above it, so it cannot match. The /18 at 64 spans 16384 to 32767 and contains 27974. The /16 contains it too but is wider, so the narrower range wins.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: GATE CSE 2025 Set 1 question 40
GATE 2025 CS-1 final answer key, IIT Roorkee (organising institute)

hints.text: More than one table entry may contain this destination. How does a router choose among several that match?
Each entry is a prefix: an address belongs to it when its first N bits equal the prefix bits.
When several prefixes match, the router uses the one with the most bits, because it describes the smallest and most specific group of addresses.

Write the third octet of the destination in binary and compare it, bit by bit, with the third octet of each entry up to that entry prefix length. The first two octets are fixed by every entry with a prefix of at least 16.
The third octet 109 is 01101101, so it begins with bit 0, which rules out any entry whose third octet starts with 1.

variation.stem: A packet with destination address 172.20.100.5 arrives at a router with this table: 172.20.0.0/16 to E1; 172.20.64.0/18 to E2; 172.20.96.0/19 to E3; 172.20.77.0/24 to E4; default to E5. Which interface is the packet forwarded to?
variation.explanation: The /16, the /18 (third octet 64 to 127) and the /19 (96 to 127) all contain third octet 100. The /24 needs third octet 77, so it does not match, and the default is only a fallback. The longest matching prefix is the /19, so the packet goes to E3.

questions.stem:
Suppose a message of size 15000 bytes is transmitted from a source to a destination using IPv4 protocol via two routers as shown in the figure. Each router has a defined maximum transmission unit (MTU) as shown in the figure, including IP header.
The number of fragments that will be delivered to the destination is ________ . (Answer in integer)
questions.figure: Source, then Router-1 (MTU = 5000 bytes), then Router-2 (MTU = 3000 bytes), then Destination, connected in a line. Each MTU includes the IP header.

diagram.alt: Source connected to Router-1 with MTU 5000 bytes, then Router-2 with MTU 3000 bytes, then Destination.

solutionDiagram.alt: Bars of the 15000 data bytes cut into 4976, 4976, 4976, 72 after Router-1 and into seven fragments after Router-2.

steps.title: Terms and rules
steps.body: Fragmentation cuts an IP datagram into pieces small enough for a link's MTU (maximum packet size, header included). Each fragment has a 20-byte header, so it carries at most MTU - 20 data bytes, rounded down to a multiple of 8 because the offset field counts in 8-byte units (only the last fragment may break this). A router that receives fragments and meets a smaller MTU cuts each fragment again; nobody reassembles until the destination.

steps.title: First link, MTU 5000
steps.body: Data per fragment: $5000-20=4980$, rounded down to a multiple of 8 is 4976. $15000 = 3\times4976 + 72$. So 3 full fragments of 4976 and one of 72 data bytes: 4 fragments.

steps.title: Second link, MTU 3000
steps.body: Data per fragment: $3000-20=2980$, rounded down to 2976. Each 4976-byte fragment becomes $2976+2000$, two fragments. The 72-byte fragment already fits, so it stays one fragment.

steps.title: Count
steps.body: Three big fragments give $3\times2=6$ fragments, plus 1 small one: 7 reach the destination.

shortcut.body: Fragments of 4976, 4976, 4976, 72 become 2 + 2 + 2 + 1. Rounding to a multiple of 8 does not change the count here, but do it anyway. 2.5 minutes.

traps.text: 4 or 5: counting only fragments produced at one router.
6: forgetting the small 72-byte last piece that is left over from the first fragmentation.

recognize.clues: Two routers in a row with different MTUs and a count of fragments at the destination show that fragments are fragmented again hop by hop, with no reassembly between.
recognize.contrast: A single-link question fragments once; with a second smaller MTU the piece sizes change per hop, so the count is not the data length divided by the smallest MTU.

check.body: Add the data bytes at the destination: three fragments split into 2976 + 2000 give 3 x 4976 = 14928, and the short piece of 72 brings the total to 15000, so no byte is lost. Each arriving packet fits the 3000 MTU: 2996, 2020 and 92 bytes with their headers.

sources.label: GATE Overflow: GATE CSE 2025 Set 1 question 57
GATE 2025 CS-1 final answer key, IIT Roorkee (organising institute)

hints.text: Does a fragment get fragmented again if a later link has a smaller MTU? And does anyone put the pieces back together on the way?
Fragments are independent packets. A router meeting a smaller MTU cuts each fragment further, and only the destination reassembles.
Each piece carries a 20-byte header, so it holds at most MTU minus 20 data bytes, rounded down to a multiple of 8 except for the last piece of a datagram.
Split the 15000 bytes for the first MTU, then split each resulting piece separately for the second MTU, and add up the pieces.
The first link allows 4980 data bytes, which rounds down to 4976, so the datagram becomes three full fragments and one short one.

variation.stem: A message of 10000 bytes is sent by IPv4 from a source via two routers to a destination. The first link has MTU 4000 bytes and the second link has MTU 2500 bytes, both including the 20-byte IP header. The number of fragments delivered to the destination is ________. (Answer in integer)
variation.explanation: The first link carries 3976 data bytes per fragment, so the 10000 bytes become pieces of 3976, 3976, 2048. The second link carries 2480 data bytes, so each 3976 piece splits in two and the 2048-byte piece stays whole. That gives 2 + 2 + 1 = 5 fragments.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about IPv4 fragmentation is/are TRUE?
options: The fragmentation of an IP datagram is performed only at the source of the datagram
The fragmentation of an IP datagram is performed at any IP router which finds that the size of the datagram to be transmitted exceeds the MTU
The reassembly of fragments is performed only at the destination of the datagram
The reassembly of fragments is performed at all intermediate routers along the path from the source to the destination

steps.title: Terms
steps.body: Fragmentation is cutting a datagram into smaller datagrams because the next link has a smaller MTU (maximum packet size). Reassembly is joining the pieces back. In IPv4 the routers in the middle cut when they must, but only the final receiver joins.

steps.title: Check statements
steps.body: (A) False: the source may fragment, but so can any router that finds the datagram too big for the outgoing link. (B) True: that is exactly what IPv4 routers do (if the DF bit is not set). (C) True: fragments may take different paths, so only the destination is sure to see them all. (D) False: reassembling at each router would waste time, and later links may force the pieces apart again.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Statements B and C are true; A and D are false.

shortcut.body: IPv4: any router fragments, only the destination reassembles. 10 seconds.

traps.text: Selecting A: the source is not the only place that fragments; that is IPv6 behaviour, where routers never fragment.
Selecting D: intermediate routers forward fragments unchanged; reassembly there is not done.

recognize.clues: The words "fragmentation" and "reassembly" with "at the source", "any IP router" and "destination" ask where each job is done in IPv4.
recognize.contrast: IPv6 lets only the source fragment and routers never do; the question says IPv4, where a router that meets a smaller MTU cuts the datagram itself.

check.body: Take a 1000-byte datagram that the source sends over a link with MTU 1500, then a router meets a second link with MTU 600. The source could not have known about that second link, so the router must cut the datagram: A is false and B is true. For C and D, the pieces made there may leave by different routes, so no middle router is sure to hold all of them, and a router that joined them would only have to cut them again at the next small MTU. So C is true and D is false.

questions.stem: Which of the following fields of an IP header is/are always modified by any router before it forwards the IP packet?

steps.title: Terms
steps.body: A router forwards a packet toward its destination; it must not change who sent it or what it carries. TTL (time to live) is a hop counter that every router decrements by 1, so that packets cannot loop forever. The header checksum is a check over the header bits.

steps.title: Apply
steps.body: Source address: unchanged (only a NAT device changes it). Protocol: unchanged, it names the payload type. TTL: always decremented by 1. Header checksum: it covers the TTL, so changing TTL forces the router to recompute it every time.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: TTL and Header Checksum: options C and D.

shortcut.body: Every router lowers TTL, and because TTL is in the header, the checksum changes too. 10 seconds.

traps.text: Selecting Source IP: only a NAT box rewrites it, an ordinary router never does.
Selecting Protocol: it describes the payload and stays the same hop to hop.
Leaving out checksum: it is easy to treat it as untouched, but it must change whenever TTL does.

recognize.clues: "Fields of an IP header" with "always modified by any router" asks which header fields change hop by hop in plain forwarding.
recognize.contrast: A NAT device also rewrites addresses, but that is a special middlebox and not what any router does; the word "any router" rules it out.

check.body: Send a packet across three routers. Its source address and protocol are the same at the destination as at the start, while TTL has dropped by 3. The checksum is computed over the header including TTL, so a changed TTL gives a different checksum value at every hop.

questions.stem: Which one of the following CIDR prefixes exactly represents the range of IP addresses 10.12.2.0 to 10.12.3.255?

solutionDiagram.alt: Third octet values 0 to 3 as columns; the /23 bar covers exactly 2 and 3, the /24 bar only 2, the /22 bar all of 0 to 3.

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: A CIDR block address/p covers $2^{32-p}$ consecutive addresses starting at an address whose last $32-p$ bits are 0. A prefix "exactly represents" a range when the block starts at the range's first address and ends at its last.

steps.title: Size of the range
steps.body: 10.12.2.0 to 10.12.3.255 covers third octets 2 and 3, each with 256 addresses: $2\times256=512=2^9$. So 9 host bits, prefix $32-9=23$.

steps.title: Check options
steps.body: (A) 10.12.2.0/23: starts at 10.12.2.0, 512 addresses, ends at 10.12.3.255. Exact. (B) /24 covers only 10.12.2.0 to 10.12.2.255, too small. (C) 10.12.0.0/22 covers 10.12.0.0 to 10.12.3.255, too big. (D) /22 needs the third octet to be a multiple of 4, but 2 is not, so this is not a valid block. Answer (A).

shortcut.body: Count addresses: 512 = $2^9$, so /23. The start must be divisible by 2 in the third octet: 2 is. 30 seconds.

traps.text: /24 gives 256 addresses and misses 10.12.3.x.
10.12.0.0/22 includes the range but also 10.12.0.0 to 10.12.1.255, which are outside it.
10.12.2.0/22 uses the right start with the wrong prefix; the start is not aligned to 1024 addresses.

recognize.clues: A start address and an end address are given, and a single prefix must cover them "exactly"; that is a size and alignment test on a CIDR block.
recognize.contrast: Route aggregation also merges blocks, but here there is nothing to merge: one range must be matched to one prefix, so it is only size plus alignment.

check.body: Expand 10.12.2.0/23 back: it holds $2^{9}=512$ addresses, so the last one is 10.12.2.0 + 511 = 10.12.3.255, which is the end of the range, and the third octet 2 is a multiple of 2, so the block is aligned. Try 10.12.2.0/24 the same way: it ends at 10.12.2.255, short of 10.12.3.255.

A CIDR block with prefix length $p$ holds $2^{32-p}$ consecutive addresses, and its first address has all $32-p$ host bits equal to 0.
Count how many addresses the range holds. That count fixes the prefix length, and then the starting address must be a multiple of the block size.
Only the third octet changes across the range, so count its values, multiply by the 256 addresses per value, then write that as a power of 2.
The range has a whole number of 256-address groups, a power of two. Take the logarithm to base 2 of the total to get the number of host bits.

questions.stem: Which of the following fields is/are modified in the IP header of a packet going out of a network address translation (NAT) device from an internal network to an external network?

steps.title: Terms
steps.body: NAT (network address translation) lets many hosts with private addresses share one public address. For a packet leaving the network, the NAT device replaces the private source address (and the port) with its own public address, and remembers the mapping so that replies can be translated back.

steps.title: Which fields change
steps.body: Source IP: replaced by the public address. Destination IP: unchanged, it is where the packet is going. Header checksum: it covers the source address, so it must be recomputed after the change. Total length: the replacement address is again 4 bytes, so the packet size is unchanged.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Source IP and Header Checksum: A and C.

shortcut.body: Outgoing NAT rewrites the source; any header change forces a new checksum. Destination and length stay. 15 seconds.

traps.text: Selecting Destination IP: that is rewritten only for packets coming in (or by destination NAT), not for outgoing packets.
Selecting Total Length: address substitution is same-size, so length does not change.
Omitting Header Checksum: it is easy to forget because it is not an address, but it covers the changed source.

recognize.clues: "Going out of a NAT device from an internal network to an external network" fixes the direction, so the question is which header fields are rewritten for an outgoing packet.
recognize.contrast: For an incoming reply the NAT device rewrites the destination instead; the direction in the stem decides which address is touched.

check.body: Compare the two directions. A reply arriving from outside is addressed to the public address and must be turned back to the private host, so the field rewritten on the way in is the other address. That confirms that on the way out the sender side is the one replaced. Total length cannot change because a 4-byte address is replaced by another 4-byte address.

questions.stem:
Consider the entries shown below in the forwarding table of an IP router. Each entry consists of an IP prefix and the corresponding next hop router for packets whose destination IP address matches the prefix. The notation “/N” in a prefix indicates a subnet mask with the most significant N bits set to 1.
This router forwards 20 packets each to 5 hosts. The IP addresses of the hosts are 10.1.1.16, 10.1.1.72, 10.1.1.132, 10.1.1.191, and 10.1.1.205 . The number of packets forwarded via the next hop router R2 is _______

solutionDiagram.alt: Last octet 0 to 255 with bars for the /24 (R1), /26 64-127 (R3), /25 128-255 (R2) and /26 192-255 (R4) and ticks at the five host addresses.

steps.title: Rule: longest prefix match
steps.body: An address matches an entry when its first N bits equal the prefix. When several entries match, the router uses the one with the largest N. A /24 here fixes 10.1.1 and leaves the last octet free; a /25 splits that octet in two halves of 128; a /26 splits it in four quarters of 64.

steps.title: Place each host
steps.body: .16: only the /24 matches, R1. .72: in 64 to 127, /26 beats /24, R3. .132: in 128 to 255, but below 192, so /25 beats /24 and R4 misses, R2. .191: 191 is below 192, so R4 does not match; /25 gives R2. .205: in 192 to 255, the /26 beats the /25, R4.

steps.title: Count
steps.body: Hosts using R2: .132 and .191, at 20 packets each: $2\times20=40$.

shortcut.body: Draw the 0 to 255 line: R2 owns 128 to 255 except 192 to 255 which R4 takes, so R2 gets 128 to 191. Hosts .132 and .191 fall there: 2 x 20 = 40. 1 minute.

traps.text: 60: counting .205 for R2 because it lies inside the /25 range 128 to 255; the longer /26 of R4 takes it.
20: missing that 191 is the last address below 192 and still belongs to R2.

recognize.clues: A forwarding table with prefixes of different lengths, and destination addresses to be sent through it, is a longest prefix match problem.
recognize.contrast: Subnetting splits one block into equal pieces; here the blocks overlap and nest, so the choice between them is made by prefix length and not by splitting.

check.body: Second route by intervals: R4 owns last-octet 192 to 255, so R2 keeps only 128 to 191 of its /25. Of the five hosts (16, 72, 132, 191, 205), only 132 and 191 lie in 128 to 191, so $2\times20=40$. The other three fall in /24 (16), /26 64 to 127 (72) and /26 192 to 255 (205), none of which is R2.

hints.text: Each host has its own best-matching entry, and the question asks only about one next hop. Plan to decide the match host by host.
A prefix /N matches an address when the first N bits agree. A larger N means a smaller, more specific block of addresses.
When several entries match an address, the router uses the one with the longest prefix. A host inside a big block can still be taken by a smaller block nested inside it.
All prefixes share the first three octets, so only the last octet matters. Write each entry as a range of last-octet values, then place every host in the ranges.
The /26 entries cut the last octet into quarters of 64 and the /25 into halves of 128. Mark where each quarter begins before you look at the hosts.

variation.stem: A router has these forwarding entries: 10.2.0.0/16 via A, 10.2.128.0/17 via B, 10.2.128.0/18 via C and 10.2.224.0/19 via D. questions.stem: Consider sending an IP datagram of size 1420 bytes (including 20 bytes of IP header) from a sender to a receiver over a path of two links with a router between them. The first link (sender to router) has an MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) size of 542 bytes, while the second link (router to receiver) has an MTU size of 360 bytes. The number of fragments that would be delivered at the receiver is ________

solutionDiagram.alt: Bars of 1400 data bytes cut into 520, 520, 360 on the first link and into 336, 184, 336, 184, 336, 24 on the second.

steps.title: Terms and rules
steps.body: MTU is the largest IP packet, header included, a link can carry. A datagram larger than the MTU is cut into fragments; each has a 20-byte header, so carries at most MTU - 20 data bytes, rounded down to a multiple of 8 (offsets count in 8-byte units). The router that meets the second, smaller MTU cuts the fragments again.

steps.title: Data to send
steps.body: Datagram 1420 bytes with a 20-byte header: $1420-20=1400$ data bytes.

steps.title: Link 1, MTU 542
steps.body: $542-20=522$, rounded down to a multiple of 8 is 520. $1400=520+520+360$: three fragments with data 520, 520, 360.

steps.title: Link 2, MTU 360
steps.body: $360-20=340$, rounded down to 336. A 520 fragment becomes $336+184$ (two fragments); the 360 fragment becomes $336+24$ (two fragments). Total: $2+2+2=6$ fragments reach the receiver.

shortcut.body: Per link, data per fragment = largest multiple of 8 not above MTU - 20: 520, then 336. 1400 gives 3 pieces; 520 and 360 each need 2 on 336. 3 x 2 = 6. 2 minutes.

traps.text: 5: forgetting that the 360-byte last piece (which exceeds 336) must be split again.
3: counting only the fragments produced by the first link.

recognize.clues: A datagram size, a header size and two MTUs on consecutive links ask for a count of fragments, which is the fragmentation arithmetic repeated at the second link.
recognize.contrast: Fragmenting once for a single link is a plain division; with two links the pieces from the first link may be split again, so the count is not the second division of the original data.

check.body: Add the data bytes of the final fragments. They must sum to the original data size, since fragmentation loses nothing. Also check that every fragment but the last has a data size divisible by 8 and that every fragment plus its header fits within the MTU of the link it last crossed.

GATE 2024 CS1 final answer key (organising institute IISc Bengaluru), GATE archive copy on the IIT Guwahati site

hints.text: The datagram passes two links with different MTUs, so it is cut twice. Count the pieces that arrive, not the pieces made on the first link.
MTU is the biggest IP packet a link carries, header included. Each fragment gets its own 20-byte header, so it carries less data than the MTU.
The fragment offset is stored in units of 8 bytes, so the data in every fragment except the last must be a multiple of 8. Round the room left after the header down to such a multiple.
First remove the header to get the data bytes. Cut that data for link 1, then cut each resulting fragment again for link 2, keeping the fragments that already fit as they are.
The data is 1400 bytes. On link 1 each fragment has room for 542 - 20 = 522 bytes of data, and the nearest multiple of 8 below that is the fragment size to use.

variation.stem: An IP datagram of 1820 bytes (including a 20-byte header) travels from a sender through a router to a receiver. The first link has MTU 532 bytes and the second link has MTU 332 bytes. The number of fragments delivered at the receiver is ______
variation.explanation: Data is 1800 bytes. On the first link the data per fragment is 512, giving 512, 512, 512 and 264. On the second link the room is 312, so each 512 splits into 312 and 200, while 264 already fits. That is $3\times2+1=7$ fragments.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is/are INCORRECT about the OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) routing protocol used in the Internet?
options: OSPF implements Bellman-Ford algorithm to find shortest paths.
OSPF uses Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm to implement least-cost path routing.
OSPF is used as an inter-domain routing protocol.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: A routing protocol is how routers learn the best path to every network. There are two families. Distance vector: each router tells its neighbours its table of distances, and each router runs the Bellman-Ford update on what it hears (RIP is the example). Link state: each router floods the state of its own links to every router, so all routers hold the same map, and each runs Dijkstra's algorithm on that map (OSPF is the example). An autonomous system (AS) is a set of networks under one administration. A protocol used inside one AS is intra-domain (interior); a protocol used between ASs is inter-domain (exterior, BGP is the example). The rule for this question: OSPF = link state + Dijkstra + intra-domain + areas. The question asks for the statements that are INCORRECT, so the answer is the set of false statements.

steps.title: Check each statement
steps.body: (A) says OSPF uses Bellman-Ford. Bellman-Ford is the distance vector computation. OSPF is link state and uses Dijkstra, so (A) is incorrect. (B) says OSPF uses Dijkstra's algorithm for least-cost paths. That is exactly what OSPF does on its link-state database, so (B) is correct. (C) says OSPF is an inter-domain protocol. OSPF runs inside one AS (it is an interior gateway protocol); the inter-domain protocol of the Internet is BGP. So (C) is incorrect. (D) says OSPF implements hierarchical routing. OSPF splits an AS into areas that connect through a backbone area (area 0), so routing is hierarchical and (D) is correct.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The incorrect statements are (A) and (C). In the exam an MSQ scores only when exactly the right set is chosen, so select A and C and nothing else.

shortcut.body: OSPF = "Open" + "Shortest Path First" = link state = Dijkstra, inside one AS, with areas. Bellman-Ford belongs to RIP and inter-domain belongs to BGP, so A and C are the false ones. 30 seconds.

traps.text: Marking (B) as incorrect: Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm is exactly what OSPF runs, so (B) is a true statement and must not be selected.
Marking (D) as incorrect: OSPF does use areas with a backbone area, which is hierarchical routing, so (D) is true.
Selecting only (A) or only (C): both are incorrect, and an MSQ gives no credit for a partial set. Reading the stem as "which are correct" is the usual reason for picking B and D instead.

recognize.clues: The statements name OSPF with Bellman-Ford, Dijkstra, inter-domain and hierarchical routing; each is a fact that separates link state from distance vector.
recognize.contrast: RIP is distance vector with Bellman-Ford; OSPF is link state with Dijkstra. BGP, not OSPF, is the protocol between domains.

check.body: Check all four against the name and the scope. "Shortest Path First" names Dijkstra, so B is true and A, which says Bellman-Ford, is false. OSPF messages carry an area number and run inside one AS, while the protocol between ASs is BGP, so C is false. Area 0 joins the other areas, so D is true. The false set is A and C.

questions.stem: The forwarding table of a router is shown below. A packet addressed to a destination address 200.150.68.118 arrives at the router. It will be forwarded to the interface with ID ______.

solutionDiagram.alt: Two number lines. Third octet 0 to 255: the /16, /19 (64 to 95) and /24 (68 only) rows all contain 68. Last octet 0 to 255: the /24 covers all, the /27 covers 64 to 95, and the marker at 118 is outside the /27.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: A forwarding table lists routes as a subnet number plus a subnet mask. The mask has 1s for the network part and 0s for the host part; the number of 1s is the prefix length, written /n. A destination address matches a row when the destination and the subnet number are equal on every bit where the mask has a 1. Several rows can match at once. The rule is longest prefix match: among all matching rows, the router uses the one with the largest prefix length, because it describes the smallest and most specific group of addresses. The Default row matches everything and is used only when no other row matches.

steps.title: Turn each mask into a prefix and a range
Test the destination against each row
steps.body: The destination is 200.150.68.118. Row 1 (/16): 200.150 matches, so it matches. Row 2 (/19): the third octet 68 lies in 64 to 95, so it matches. Row 3 (/24): 200.150.68 matches, so it matches. Row 4 (/27): the fourth octet 118 must lie in 64 to 95, but 118 is larger, so it does not match. Three rows match: /16, /19 and /24.

steps.title: Pick the longest prefix
steps.body: Among /16, /19 and /24 the longest is /24, which is row 3, so the packet is forwarded to interface 3. The /27 row looks more specific but never applies here. Answer: 3.

shortcut.body: Write the destination's third and fourth octets, 68 and 118. Check the most specific row first: /27 covers fourth octet 64 to 95, 118 is outside, drop it. Next /24 for 200.150.68.x matches, so interface 3. 1 minute. Always check the longest rows first and stop at the first match, but make sure you converted masks like 224 correctly.

traps.text: Answering 4: the /27 row is the most specific in the table, but its range ends at 95, and 118 is outside it. A row only counts if the destination really falls in its range.
Answering 2: the /19 row matches too, but a shorter prefix (19) loses to the /24 that also matches.
Answering 1 or 0: taking the first row that matches, or falling back to the default, ignores the rule that the longest matching prefix wins.

recognize.clues: A forwarding table with masks of different lengths, a Default row and one destination address asks for the longest matching prefix.
recognize.contrast: The most specific looking row is not always the winner: a longer prefix only wins if the destination actually falls inside its range.

check.body: Row 3: 200.150.68.118 AND 255.255.255.0 = 200.150.68.0, equal to its subnet number, so it matches. Row 4: 118 is 01110110 and 224 is 11100000, so 118 AND 224 = 01100000 = 96, giving 200.150.68.96, which is not 200.150.68.64, so the longer /27 row does not match.

hints.text: Several rows may fit this destination at the same time. Decide how the router chooses among them before you test any row.
A mask of ones followed by zeros gives a prefix length, the count of leading ones. A destination matches a row when it agrees with the subnet number on every bit the mask marks with a 1.
Among all rows that match, the router uses the one with the longest prefix. The Default row is used only when nothing else matches.

The mask byte 224 is 11100000, which has three ones. In the third octet that makes the mask 255.255.224.0 a /19, and in the fourth octet it makes 255.255.255.224 a /27.

questions.stem: Consider an enterprise network with two Ethernet segments, a web server and a firewall, connected via three routers as shown below. What is the number of subnets inside the enterprise network?
questions.figure: A firewall has a link labelled To Internet going out of the enterprise. The firewall is joined by one link to the left router and by another link to the top router. The top router is joined to the web server and to the right router. The left router is joined to an Ethernet segment with several hosts; the right router is joined to a second Ethernet segment with several hosts.

diagram.alt: Firewall with a dashed To Internet line, links from the firewall to a left router and a top router, the top router joined to a web server and to a right router, and the left and right routers each joined to an Ethernet segment with hosts.

solutionDiagram.alt: The same network with the six links and segments numbered 1 to 6: firewall to left router, firewall to top router, top router to web server, top router to right router, and the two Ethernet segments. The Internet line is marked as outside.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: A subnet is a group of interfaces that can reach each other directly, without passing through a router, and so share one network prefix. A router sits between subnets: each of its interfaces is on a different subnet. Every point-to-point link between two devices is its own subnet, and a whole Ethernet segment (hosts on one shared cable or switch) is one subnet. The rule: count the links and segments, not the boxes. A link that leaves the enterprise, such as the one to the Internet, is not inside the enterprise network.

steps.title: List every link and segment
steps.body: From the figure: (1) firewall to the left router; (2) firewall to the top router; (3) top router to the web server; (4) top router to the right router; (5) left router to its Ethernet segment; (6) right router to its Ethernet segment. The line "To Internet" leaves the firewall outward, so it is not inside the enterprise network and is not counted. The hosts on an Ethernet segment all share that segment's subnet, so they add nothing.

steps.title: Count
steps.body: Six links or segments give six subnets. Answer: 6, option (C).

shortcut.body: Count lines between devices, ignoring the line to the Internet, and count each Ethernet segment once: 4 router or server links plus 2 Ethernet segments = 6. 40 seconds.

traps.text: Answering 3 counts the routers. A router is not a subnet; it joins subnets, and each interface of a router sits in a different one.
Answering 12 counts interfaces (two per link, and two ends of each Ethernet attachment). Both ends of one link belong to the same subnet, so count the link once.
Answering 8 counts devices (firewall, three routers, web server, two segments) and the Internet. The count is of links and segments inside the enterprise.

recognize.clues: The words "number of subnets" with a figure of routers, a firewall, a web server and Ethernet segments say that the count comes from the topology: every router interface marks a boundary between subnets.
recognize.contrast: This is not a prefix-length question about how many hosts a subnet holds. No addresses are given, so only the drawing decides, and the line to the Internet is not part of the enterprise.

check.body: Count interface ends instead of lines. Inside the enterprise the firewall has 2 interfaces, the left router 2, the top router 3, the right router 2 and the web server 1, which is 10. The two Ethernet segments take one router interface each, and the other 8 ends pair up on point-to-point links, giving 4 links plus 2 segments.

questions.stem: Consider routing table of an organization's router shown below: Which of the following prefixes in CIDR notation can be collectively used to correctly aggregate all of the subnets in the routing table?

solutionDiagram.alt: Third octet 160 to 175. Top: the four subnets as bars covering 164 to 167, 166 to 167, 168 to 169 and 170 to 171. Bottom: the two /22 aggregates 164 to 167 and 168 to 171 shaded, against the wider /20 and /21 blocks that start at 160.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: A CIDR prefix a.b.c.d/n fixes the first n bits; the last 32 - n bits are host bits and must be 0 in the written address. So a prefix is valid only when its host bits are all 0, which means its block starts at a multiple of the block size. Route aggregation (supernetting) replaces several routes by fewer prefixes that together cover all of them. A correct aggregate has to cover every listed subnet and should not claim addresses outside them. The mask 255.255.252.0 is /22 (the third octet 252 = 11111100 has 6 ones: 16 + 6) and 255.255.254.0 is /23 (254 has 7 ones).

steps.title: Write each subnet as a range of the third octet
steps.body: 12.20.164.0/22 covers third octets 164 to 167 (4 values). 12.20.170.0/23 covers 170 to 171 (2 values). 12.20.168.0/23 covers 168 to 169. 12.20.166.0/23 covers 166 to 167, which lies inside 164.0/22. The union is the unbroken range 164 to 171: 8 values of the third octet, 8 x 256 = 2048 addresses.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.body: (B) 12.20.164.0/22: a /22 block spans 4 values of the third octet, so it must start at a multiple of 4. 164 = 4 x 41, valid, covers 164 to 167. (D) 12.20.168.0/22: 168 = 4 x 42, valid, covers 168 to 171. Together B and D cover 164 to 171 exactly, no more and no less. (C) 12.20.164.0/21: a /21 spans 8 values and must start at a multiple of 8, but 164 = 8 x 20 + 4, so as written it has nonzero host bits and is not a valid prefix. The real /21 containing 164 is 12.20.160.0/21, covering 160 to 167, which misses 168 to 171. (A) 12.20.164.0/20: a /20 spans 16 values and starts at a multiple of 16, and 164 is not one. The /20 containing 164 is 12.20.160.0/20, covering 160 to 175. It would include the subnets, but also 160 to 163 and 172 to 175, which the organization does not own, so it does not aggregate them correctly.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The collective aggregate is B and D: 12.20.164.0/22 and 12.20.168.0/22. Answer: options (B) and (D).

shortcut.body: Third octets run 164 to 171, eight values. A /21 would have to start at 160 or 168, so 164 cannot start one. Split into two blocks of 4 starting at 164 and 168: two /22s, B and D. 2 minutes. Unsafe if you skip the alignment test: a /20 or /21 that starts at 164 looks like a cover but is not a valid prefix.

traps.text: Selecting 12.20.164.0/20: it seems to be the one big prefix that covers everything, but 164 is not a multiple of 16, and the real block 160 to 175 also claims 160 to 163 and 172 to 175.
Selecting 12.20.164.0/21: the size looks right (8 values) but the start 164 is not a multiple of 8. The block starting at 160 would end at 167 and miss 168 to 171.
Selecting only B or only D: each covers just half of 164 to 171. The question says "collectively", so both prefixes are needed.

recognize.clues: The question asks which prefixes can "collectively aggregate" the entries of a routing table written with masks, so the method is supernetting: merge the address ranges, then test each candidate prefix for coverage and alignment.
recognize.contrast: Longest prefix match picks one route for a single destination. Here no destination is given: the task is to merge routes, and a block that also covers addresses nobody owns is not a correct aggregate.

check.body: Compare address counts. The routes cover 8 values of the third octet, which is 8 x 256 = 2048 addresses. Two /22 blocks hold 1024 + 1024 = 2048, an exact fit, while a /20 holds 4096, twice as much as the organization owns.

questions.stem: Consider a network with three routers P, Q, R shown in the figure below. All the links have cost of unity. The routers exchange distance vector routing information and have converged on the routing tables, after which the link Q−R fails. Assume that P and Q send out routing updates at random times, each at the same average rate. The probability of a routing loop formation (rounded off to one decimal place) between P and Q, leading to count-to-infinity problem, is ______.
questions.figure: Three routers in a row: P is joined to Q, and Q is joined to R. Every link has cost 1.

diagram.alt: Three boxes P, Q and R in a line, joined P to Q and Q to R, each link labelled cost 1.

solutionDiagram.alt: Two cases after Q to R fails. Case 1, P sends its update first, telling Q that R is at cost 2: Q adopts a route through P and a loop forms. Case 2, Q sends first, telling P that R is infinite: P agrees and no loop forms. Each case has probability one half.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: In distance vector routing each router keeps, for every destination, a cost and a next hop. Periodically it sends its whole table to its neighbours. On receiving a neighbour's table, a router computes cost = link cost + the neighbour's advertised cost, and adopts it if it is cheaper than what it has, or if that neighbour is already its next hop for that destination (it must follow its next hop's news, good or bad). Count to infinity: after a failure two routers each believe the other can reach the lost destination, so they keep handing the route back and forth and the cost climbs by 1 each round. The question asks for the probability that the first update after the failure creates such a loop.

steps.title: The converged state and the failure
steps.body: Before the failure P reaches R at cost 2 through Q; Q reaches R at cost 1 directly. When Q−R fails, only Q notices. Q has no other route, so it sets its cost to R to infinity. P has not heard anything and still holds "R at cost 2 via Q". Nothing changes until one of P or Q sends its next update.

steps.title: The two possible orders
steps.body: If P sends first, it tells Q "R at cost 2". Q sees 1 + 2 = 3, which beats infinity, and adopts R via P at cost 3. Now Q's next hop for R is P while P's next hop for R is Q: a loop. Q then advertises 3, P follows its next hop and moves to 4, Q to 5, and so on up to infinity. If Q sends first, it tells P "R is unreachable". P's next hop for R is Q, so P adopts infinity too. Both now agree and there is no loop.

steps.title: Probability
steps.body: The two updates are independent and happen at the same average rate, so either one is equally likely to come first. A loop forms exactly when P comes first. So the probability is 1/2 = 0.5. Answer: 0.5.

shortcut.body: Loop if and only if P speaks before Q. Two symmetric random events: 1/2 = 0.5. 1 minute. Unsafe if the protocol uses split horizon with poisoned reverse: then P never advertises R back to Q, there is no loop, and the probability would be 0. The question assumes plain distance vector.

traps.text: Answering 1: assuming a failure always ends in count to infinity. If Q's "unreachable" update reaches P first, the bad news spreads correctly and no loop forms.
Answering 0: assuming split horizon or that both routers learn of the failure at the same instant. The question says plain distance vector with random update times.
Answering 0.25 or 0.3: multiplying probabilities as if two separate events had to happen. Only one comparison matters, which of the two routers speaks first.

recognize.clues: A link fails, the two surviving routers send updates at random times, and the question asks for the probability of a loop leading to count-to-infinity: a race between two periodic updates.
recognize.contrast: This is not a question about convergence time or about split horizon. Nothing in the stem adds loop prevention, so plain distance vector is assumed and the order of the updates is the only thing that matters.

check.body: Enumerate the two orders and name Q's table. If Q speaks first, P learns that R is unreachable and no stale route is passed on, so there is no loop. If P speaks first, Q has lost R and accepts P's stale route to R at cost 3 through P, while P still sends R-bound packets to Q, so a loop forms. Exactly one of the two orders loops, and with equal rates each order is equally likely.

hints.text: After the link fails, which router knows about it, and what does the other router still believe about R?
In distance vector routing a router adopts a neighbour's advertised cost plus its link cost, and it always follows the news from its own next hop.
A loop forms only when one router passes a stale route to a router that accepts it as a cheap way back through the sender. Which update arrives first decides whether that happens.
Trace the two orders separately: P sends first, and Q sends first. For each, write what the table of the receiving router says about R after that one update, then ask how likely each order is.
If Q speaks first it tells P that R is unreachable, and P's next hop for R is Q. Work out what P does with that, then trace the other order.

variation.stem: Three routers P, Q, R are in a row with P joined to Q and Q joined to R, all link costs 1, and the tables have converged. Then the link Q-R fails. P sends routing updates at an average rate three times that of Q, and both send at random times. What is the probability, rounded to two decimal places, that a loop forms between P and Q and leads to count-to-infinity?
variation.explanation: A loop forms exactly when P sends its stale route for R before Q reports R unreachable. For independent random timers, the chance that P comes first is its rate over the sum of the rates, 3/(3 + 1) = 0.75.

questions.stem: Consider a computer network using the distance vector routing algorithm in its network layer. The partial topology of the network is as shown below. The objective is to find the shortest-cost path from the router R to routers P and Q. Assume that R does not initially know the shortest routes to P and Q. Assume that R has three neighbouring routers denoted as X, Y, and Z. During one iteration, R measures its distance to its neighbours X, Y, and Z as 3, 2, and 5, respectively. Router R gets routing vectors from its neighbours that indicate that the distance to router P from routers X, Y, and Z are 7, 6, and 5, respectively. The routing vector also indicates that the distance to router Q from routers X, Y, and Z are 4, 6, and 8, respectively. Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct with respect to the new routing table of R, after updation during this iteration?
questions.figure: Router R is joined to three neighbours X, Y and Z. Below them the network continues (shown as dots) and leads to routers Q and P.

diagram.alt: Router R at the top joined to neighbours X, Y and Z, each with dotted branches below, and routers Q and P at the bottom of the network.

solutionDiagram.alt: A table of link cost plus reported distance. To P: via X 3+7=10, via Y 2+6=8, via Z 5+5=10, best Y with cost 8. To Q: via X 3+4=7, via Y 2+6=8, via Z 5+8=13, best X with cost 7.

options: The distance from R to P will be stored as 10.
The distance from R to Q will be stored as 7.
The next hop router for a packet from R to P is Y.
The next hop router for a packet from R to Q is Z.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: In distance vector routing a router knows only the cost of its own links and the distances its neighbours report. The report from a neighbour N says "my distance to destination D is d". R cannot reach D through N for less than (cost of the link R to N) + d. This is one step of the Bellman-Ford update: for each destination R computes that sum for every neighbour, keeps the smallest, stores it as the distance, and records the neighbour that gave it as the next hop.

steps.title: Destination P
steps.body: Link costs are X = 3, Y = 2, Z = 5 and the neighbours report their distances to P as 7, 6, 5. Through X: 3 + 7 = 10. Through Y: 2 + 6 = 8. Through Z: 5 + 5 = 10. The minimum is 8 through Y. So R stores distance 8 to P with next hop Y.

steps.title: Destination Q
steps.body: The neighbours report 4, 6, 8 to Q. Through X: 3 + 4 = 7. Through Y: 2 + 6 = 8. Through Z: 5 + 8 = 13. The minimum is 7 through X. So R stores distance 7 to Q with next hop X.

steps.title: Check the options
steps.body: (A) says the distance to P is 10: it is 8, so false. (B) says the distance to Q is 7: true. (C) says the next hop to P is Y: true. (D) says the next hop to Q is Z: it is X, so false. Answer: (B) and (C).

shortcut.body: Add the link cost to each reported distance, take the row minimum. P: 10, 8, 10, so Y and 8. Q: 7, 8, 13, so X and 7. 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Option A (10) comes from X or Z, which both give 10 for P. Y is cheaper because 2 + 6 = 8.
Option D (Z) is wrong: Z gives the worst total for Q, 5 + 8 = 13. Comparing only the reported distances instead of link cost plus reported distance leads to wrong next hops.
Choosing the neighbour with the smallest reported distance to P (Z reports 5) forgets the cost of the link from R to that neighbour.

recognize.clues: R knows only the cost of its own links and the vectors its three neighbours send, and the question asks for the stored distance and next hop after one update: a single Bellman-Ford round.
recognize.contrast: This is not link-state routing. R never sees the whole topology or runs a shortest-path search; it relies only on what its neighbours report.

check.body: Substitute the stored values back. A stored distance of 7 to P would need some neighbour to report 4 (via X), 5 (via Y) or 2 (via Z); the reports are 7, 6 and 5, so none does. A stored 6 to Q would need a report of 3, 4 or 1; the reports are 4, 6 and 8, so none does. The stored 8 to P (2 + 6 via Y) and 7 to Q (3 + 4 via X) are each achieved by a real neighbour report.

variation.stem: Router R has neighbours X, Y and Z, with link costs 4, 1 and 6. The neighbours report distances to P of 5, 9 and 2, and distances to Q of 3, 7 and 5. After one distance vector update, which of the following statements is/are correct?

questions.stem: Consider the following two statements. S1: Destination MAC address of an ARP reply is a broadcast address. S2: Destination MAC address of an ARP request is a broadcast address. Which one of the following choices is correct?

solutionDiagram.alt: Sequence of two hosts on one Ethernet. Host A sends an ARP request to the broadcast MAC address ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff; host B replies with a unicast frame to A's own MAC address.

options: Both S1 and S2 are true.
S1 is true and S2 is false.
S1 is false and S2 is true.
Both S1 and S2 are false.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: Hosts on an Ethernet segment send frames using MAC addresses (48-bit link-layer addresses), but applications use IP addresses. ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) finds the MAC address that goes with an IP address on the same subnet. The broadcast MAC address is ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff; every host on the segment accepts a frame sent to it. A unicast frame is addressed to one MAC address. The rule: a sender uses broadcast when it does not know who owns the address it is asking about, and unicast once it knows.

steps.title: The request
steps.body: Host A wants the MAC address for IP 10.0.0.9 and knows nothing about who owns it. It can only ask everyone, so the ARP request goes to the broadcast address ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff. S2 is true.

steps.title: The reply
steps.body: The owner of 10.0.0.9 learns A's IP and MAC address from the request itself. It already knows exactly who asked, so it answers with a frame addressed only to A's MAC address. The reply is unicast, so S1 is false. S1 false and S2 true is option (C).

shortcut.body: ARP request: "who has this IP?" goes to everyone, so broadcast. ARP reply goes straight back to the asker, so unicast. S1 false, S2 true: option C. 20 seconds.

traps.text: Option A treats both messages as broadcast. Only the request needs to reach everyone; the reply goes to the one host that asked.
Option B swaps the two: it would mean the answer is shouted to everyone while the question is whispered to one host that is not yet known.
Option D says neither is broadcast. But the requester does not know the target's MAC address (that is why it asks), so the request cannot be unicast.

recognize.clues: Two statements about the destination MAC address of an ARP request and of an ARP reply: the clue is who knows whose MAC address at the moment each frame is sent.
recognize.contrast: Keep the two ARP messages apart. The request is a question to everyone on the segment and the reply is an answer to one host, so the same protocol uses both kinds of destination address.

check.body: Test the opposite choices for contradiction. If the request were unicast, the sender would need the very MAC address it is trying to find, which is circular. A broadcast reply would disturb every host for a message only the asker needs, and the owner already learned the asker's address from the request.

questions.stem: Consider two hosts P and Q connected through a router R. The maximum transfer unit (MTU) value of the link between P and R is 1500 bytes, and between R and Q is 820 bytes. A TCP segment of size 1400 bytes was transferred from P to Q through R, with IP identification value as 0x1234. Assume that the IP header size is 20 bytes. Further, the packet is allowed to be fragmented, i.e., Don't Fragment (DF) flag in the IP header is not set by P. Which of the following statements is/are correct?

solutionDiagram.alt: Three bars. At P: a 20-byte header and a 1400-byte TCP segment, total 1420. At R after fragmenting for MTU 820: fragment 1 with a 20-byte header and 800 data bytes (offset 0), total 820; fragment 2 with a 20-byte header and 600 data bytes (offset 100), total 620.

options: Two fragments are created at R and the IP datagram size carrying the second fragment is 620 bytes.
If the second fragment is lost, R will resend the fragment with the IP identification value 0x1234.
If the second fragment is lost, P is required to resend the whole TCP segment.
TCP destination port can be determined by analysing only the second fragment.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: MTU (maximum transfer unit) is the largest IP datagram, header included, a link can carry. If a datagram is larger than the next link's MTU and DF is not set, a router splits it into fragments. Each fragment gets its own 20-byte IP header, the same identification value, a more-fragments (MF) flag (1 on all but the last) and a fragment offset, which counts the position of the fragment's data in units of 8 bytes. So every fragment except the last carries a multiple of 8 data bytes. Fragments are put back together only by the destination host. IP does not retransmit anything; a lost fragment makes the whole datagram unusable.

steps.title: Fragment at R
steps.body: P sends a datagram of 1400 + 20 = 1420 bytes, which fits the 1500-byte link. The link R to Q allows 820, so the data per fragment is at most 820 - 20 = 800, and 800 = 8 x 100 is a multiple of 8. The 1400 bytes of data become 800 + 600, two fragments. Fragment 1: data 800, offset 0, MF = 1, size 820 bytes. Fragment 2: data 600, offset 800 / 8 = 100, MF = 0, size 600 + 20 = 620 bytes.

steps.title: Check (A) and (B)
steps.body: (A) says two fragments are created and the second datagram is 620 bytes. Both are as computed, so (A) is true. (B) says R will resend the second fragment if it is lost. A router forwards a fragment once; it keeps no copy and IP has no retransmission, so (B) is false.

steps.title: Check (C) and (D)
steps.body: (C) says P must resend the whole TCP segment if the second fragment is lost. Q cannot reassemble the datagram and drops the partial fragments after a timeout. TCP at P gets no acknowledgement, times out and resends the whole segment, so (C) is true. (D) says the TCP destination port can be found from the second fragment alone. The port is in the first bytes of the TCP header, which are in the first fragment (offset 0). The second fragment holds bytes 800 to 1399 of the segment, so (D) is false. Answer: (A) and (C).

shortcut.body: Per-fragment data = 820 - 20 = 800, so 1400 = 800 + 600 and the second datagram is 620 bytes: A true. Lost fragment means the sender's TCP resends everything: C true. Only the first fragment has the TCP header, so D false. IP routers never resend, so B false. 2 minutes.

traps.text: Option B assumes routers repair losses. A router has no memory of fragments it forwarded and IP is best effort; recovery comes from TCP at the sender, with a new datagram.
Option D forgets that only the first fragment contains the TCP header. Later fragments are just slices of data and carry no port numbers.
Forgetting the 20-byte header in the second fragment gives 600 instead of 620 and drops (A). The datagram size includes the header.

recognize.clues: Two links with different MTUs, the Don't Fragment flag left clear, an identification value, and statements about lost fragments and about which fragment holds the TCP header: a fragmentation and reassembly question.
recognize.contrast: Do not confuse this with TCP segmentation. IP splits one datagram and rejoins it only at the destination, and IP never recovers a single lost fragment, so TCP at the sender resends the whole segment.

check.body: Check the sizes add up. The data is 800 + 600 = 1400, equal to the original segment, and each fragment adds 20 bytes of header, so the two datagrams total 820 + 620 = 1440 = 1400 + 2 x 20. The second offset times 8 is 100 x 8 = 800, the length of the first fragment's data.
