questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the functionality of an IP based router. I. A router does not modify the IP packets during forwarding. II. It is not necessary for a router to implement any routing protocol. III. A router should reassemble IP fragments if the MTU of the outgoing link is larger than the size of the incoming IP packet. Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: A router joins networks and moves each IP packet one hop closer to its destination. Forwarding is the per-packet step: look up the destination in the forwarding table and send the packet out of the chosen interface. Routing is the process that builds that table, either by a routing protocol (RIP, OSPF, BGP) or by an administrator typing the entries (static routes). Fragmentation splits a datagram that is too big for a link; reassembly joins the fragments back, and for IP that happens only at the destination host. The rule: test each statement against what a router does to a packet and what it needs to run.

steps.title: Statement I
steps.body: On every hop the router decreases the TTL field by 1, and because the header changed it recomputes the header checksum. It may also fragment the packet. So the router does modify the packet, and I is false.

steps.title: Statement II
steps.body: The forwarding table can be filled by hand. A small router with static routes works with no routing protocol at all. So it is not necessary to implement one, and II is true.

steps.title: Statement III
steps.body: Reassembly is done only by the destination host, never by routers on the path; routers can forward fragments independently, and a larger MTU downstream needs no reassembly at all. So III is false. Only II is true: option (D).

shortcut.body: TTL changes on every hop, so I is false. Static routing exists, so II is true. Reassembly is the destination's job, so III is false. Answer: II only. 40 seconds.

traps.text: Option A accepts statement I. A router never forwards the packet bit for bit: the TTL goes down and the header checksum changes at every hop.
Option B claims I alone is true, which is the false statement and leaves out the true one.
Option C accepts III. Routers do not reassemble fragments even when the next link could carry the whole datagram; only the destination host reassembles.

recognize.clues: The statements are about what an IP router does to a packet, what it needs in order to run and whether it reassembles fragments: the forwarding, routing and fragmentation roles of the network layer.
recognize.contrast: Keep the router apart from the destination host. Reassembly belongs to the host and forwarding to the router, and forwarding (per packet) is a different step from routing (building the table).

check.body: Test the statements on one concrete device. A home router with only static routes forwards traffic with no routing protocol, a traceroute shows TTL running out hop by hop, which means the packet was modified, and a destination host receives the fragments separately because nothing on the path joined them.

questions.stem: An organization requires a range of IP addresses to assign one to each of its 1500 computers. The organization has approached an Internet Service Provider (ISP) for this task. The ISP uses CIDR and serves the requests from the available IP address space 202.61.0.0/17. The ISP wants to assign an address space to the organization which will minimize the number of routing entries in the ISP's router using route aggregation. Which of the following address spaces are potential candidates from which the ISP can allot any one to the organization? I. 202.61.84.0/21 II. 202.61.104.0/21 III. 202.61.64.0/21 IV. 202.61.144.0/21

solutionDiagram.alt: Third octet 0 to 159 as a number line. The ISP block covers 0 to 127. Candidate I covers 80 to 87 if aligned and is marked not aligned. Candidates II (104 to 111) and III (64 to 71) are shaded and inside the ISP block. Candidate IV (144 to 151) is outside.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: CIDR writes a block as address/p: the first p bits are the network part and the remaining 32 - p bits count the hosts, so the block holds $2^{32-p}$ addresses. A valid block must start at an address whose host bits are all 0, so its start is a multiple of its size. The ISP owns 202.61.0.0/17, which is 202.61.0.0 to 202.61.127.255: third octet 0 to 127. Anything it hands out must lie inside that range. When the ISP carves a block from its own /17, the rest of the Internet still sees only the single /17 route, so any valid block inside it keeps the routing entries minimal.

steps.title: Size needed
steps.body: 1500 hosts need at least 1500 addresses. A /22 gives $2^{10}=1024$, too few. A /21 gives $2^{11}=2048$, enough. All four candidates are /21, so size is not the filter.

steps.title: Alignment and range
steps.body: A /21 spans 8 values of the third octet, so its third octet must be a multiple of 8. I: 84 = 8 x 10 + 4, not a multiple of 8; the real block containing 84 is 202.61.80.0/21, so 202.61.84.0/21 is not a valid block. II: 104 = 8 x 13, valid, 104 to 111, inside 0 to 127. III: 64 = 8 x 8, valid, 64 to 71, inside. IV: 144 is a multiple of 8 and valid, but 144 is above 127, outside the ISP's /17, so the ISP cannot give it.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: II and III are valid blocks inside the ISP's space: option (B).

shortcut.body: Inside the /17 means third octet below 128; a /21 block starts at a multiple of 8. Check the four: 84 not a multiple of 8, 104 yes, 64 yes, 144 is above 127. So II and III. 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Option A includes I. 202.61.84.0/21 looks fine because it is a /21, but 84 is not a multiple of 8, so it is not a block boundary.
Option C includes IV. 202.61.144.0/21 is a valid /21, but it is outside the ISP's 202.61.0.0/17 range (third octet above 127).
Option D combines both errors: I is misaligned and IV is outside the ISP's space.

recognize.clues: A host count, an ISP space 202.61.0.0/17 and four candidate /21 blocks: size the block from the host count, then test alignment and containment in the ISP's range.
recognize.contrast: Subnetting splits a block the organization already owns into equal parts. Here the ISP carves a slice from its own aggregate, so the test is containment and alignment, not subnet masks for hosts.

check.body: Test the binary boundaries. A /21 block must have its low 3 bits of the third octet equal to 0. 104 is 01101000 and 64 is 01000000, so both are aligned, while 84 is 01010100 and is not. The ISP space 202.61.0.0/17 fixes only the top bit of the third octet as 0, and 144 is 10010000, whose top bit is 1, so it lies outside.

questions.stem: Consider three machines M, N, and P with IP addresses 100.10.5.2, 100.10.5.5, and 100.10.5.6 respectively. The subnet mask is set to 255.255.255.252 for all the three machines. Which one of the following is true?

solutionDiagram.alt: The last octet 0 to 11 split into three /30 blocks of four addresses: 0 to 3, 4 to 7 and 8 to 11. Markers show M at 2 in the first block, N at 5 and P at 6 both in the second block.

options: M, N, and P all belong to the same subnet
Only M and N belong to the same subnet
Only N and P belong to the same subnet
M, N, and P belong to three different subnets

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: A subnet mask has 1s for the network part and 0s for the host part. A machine's network address is its IP address ANDed bit by bit with the mask. Two machines are in the same subnet exactly when their network addresses are equal. The mask 255.255.255.252 ends in 252 = 11111100, so the last 2 bits are host bits (prefix /30) and every subnet holds 4 consecutive addresses, starting at a multiple of 4.

steps.title: AND each address with the mask
steps.body: Only the last octet changes, because the first three octets of the mask are 255. M: 2 = 00000010; AND 11111100 = 00000000 = 0, so the network is 100.10.5.0. N: 5 = 00000101; AND 11111100 = 00000100 = 4, so 100.10.5.4. P: 6 = 00000110; AND 11111100 = 00000100 = 4, so 100.10.5.4.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: N and P both have network 100.10.5.4, while M has 100.10.5.0. So only N and P belong to the same subnet. Answer: option (C).

shortcut.body: Block size 4 in the last octet: 0 to 3, 4 to 7, 8 to 11. M = 2 is in the first block; N = 5 and P = 6 are both in 4 to 7. Only N and P. 20 seconds.

traps.text: Option A ignores the mask and thinks the common prefix 100.10.5 puts all three together. With /30, the last octet matters too.
Option B pairs M and N because 2 and 5 look close. Closeness is irrelevant; the subnet is the block of four that starts at a multiple of 4, and 2 and 5 are in different blocks.
Option D says all three differ. That overlooks that 5 and 6 sit in the same block of four, 4 to 7.

recognize.clues: A subnet mask is given with three host addresses and the question asks which of them share a subnet, which means comparing network parts after masking.
recognize.contrast: CIDR aggregation also uses prefix lengths, but it merges several blocks into one route; here we only test whether addresses fall into the same block.

check.body: Rebuild the blocks from the other side: with 4 addresses per block the block boundaries are 0, 4, 8. Address 5 and address 6 both lie between 4 and 7, so they cannot be separated, while 2 lies below 4. This agrees with the AND results without repeating them.

questions.stem: Suppose that in an IP-over-Ethernet network, a machine X wishes to find the MAC address of another machine Y in its subnet. Which one of the following techniques can be used for this?
options: X sends an ARP request packet to the local gateway's IP address which then finds the MAC address of Y and sends to X
X sends an ARP request packet to the local gateway's MAC address which then finds the MAC address of Y and sends to X
X sends an ARP request packet with broadcast MAC address in its local subnet
X sends an ARP request packet with broadcast IP address in its local subnet

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: Ethernet frames are delivered by MAC address, but X only knows Y's IP address. ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) bridges that gap: X sends an ARP request asking "who has IP address of Y?", and Y answers with its MAC address. The request cannot be aimed at a particular MAC address, since the MAC is exactly what X lacks. So it is placed in an Ethernet frame whose destination is the broadcast MAC address ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, which every machine in the subnet receives. ARP works inside one subnet and travels directly in Ethernet frames, not in IP packets.

steps.title: Check the options
steps.body: (A) Sending the request to the gateway's IP address: the request is a link-layer broadcast, not an IP packet to a chosen IP address, and a gateway is only needed for machines outside the subnet. (B) Sending it to the gateway's MAC address: the gateway is not the one who holds Y's answer, and X has no reason to involve it for a machine in its own subnet. (C) An ARP request with the broadcast MAC address in the local subnet: this is the standard method, and Y replies. (D) An ARP request with a broadcast IP address: ARP is not carried in IP, and the IP broadcast address is not what the Ethernet frame is sent to. The frame needs the broadcast MAC. Answer: (C).

shortcut.body: Y is in the same subnet and X lacks its MAC, so X shouts to everyone at the link layer: broadcast MAC address. C. 20 seconds.

traps.text: Option A sends the request to the local gateway's IP. The gateway is for leaving the subnet; Y is inside it, and ARP is not sent to an IP address.
Option B aims the request at the gateway's MAC address. The sender needs to reach the owner of Y's IP, which can only be found by asking all machines, not by a single known MAC.
Option D puts the broadcast in an IP address. ARP sits directly on Ethernet, so the broadcast that matters is the Ethernet destination ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff.

recognize.clues: The machine knows only the other machine's IP and wants its MAC address inside the same subnet; that translation job is the one ARP does.
recognize.contrast: DNS also resolves a name to an address, but it maps names to IP addresses over UDP/IP; ARP maps an IP address to a MAC address directly on the local link.

check.body: Test each option against the rule that the request must work with no knowledge of Y's MAC. Any option that aims the frame at one specific MAC (the gateway) already assumes a lookup was done, and any option that uses an IP destination needs routing, which is for leaving the subnet. Only a link-wide broadcast needs nothing known in advance.

questions.stem: Consider an IP packet with a length of 4,500 bytes that includes a 20-byte IPv4 header and a 40-byte TCP header. The packet is forwarded to an IPv4 router that supports a Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) of 600 bytes. Assume that the length of the IP header in all the outgoing fragments of this packet is 20 bytes. Assume that the fragmentation offset value stored in the first fragment is 0. The fragmentation offset value stored in the third fragment is ______.

solutionDiagram.alt: Eight fragments of 4480 data bytes: seven of 576 bytes and a last one of 448. Their offsets are 0, 72, 144, 216, 288, 360, 432 and 504 units of 8 bytes; the third fragment, offset 144, is highlighted.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: MTU is the largest IP datagram, header included, that a link can carry. A router splits a bigger datagram into fragments. Each fragment has its own IP header (here 20 bytes) and a slice of the original data. The fragment offset field says where the slice starts in the original data, counted in units of 8 bytes. Because the unit is 8 bytes, every fragment except the last must carry a multiple of 8 data bytes. The rule: data per fragment = largest multiple of 8 not above (MTU - header); offset of a fragment = data bytes before it divided by 8.

steps.title: Data to be carried
steps.body: The 4500-byte packet includes its own 20-byte header. What must be carried is the rest, 4500 - 20 = 4480 bytes. The 40-byte TCP header is part of this data as far as IP is concerned.

steps.title: Data per fragment
steps.body: Each outgoing fragment can be 600 bytes with a 20-byte header, leaving 580 bytes of room. The largest multiple of 8 not above 580 is 576, which is 72 units. So fragments carry 576 bytes each, seven of them use 7 x 576 = 4032 bytes, and the eighth carries the last 448.

steps.title: Offset of the third fragment
steps.body: Before the third fragment there are two full fragments, 2 x 576 = 1152 data bytes. Its offset is 1152 / 8 = 144. The offsets of fragments 1, 2, 3 are 0, 72, 144. Answer: 144.

shortcut.body: (600 - 20) = 580, round down to a multiple of 8: 576 = 72 units. The third fragment starts after two fragments: 2 x 72 = 144. 1 minute. The total length 4500 is not needed.

traps.text: Answering 145: dividing the unrounded 580 bytes (2 x 580 / 8 = 145). The data size must be a multiple of 8, so use 576.
Answering 150: using the whole MTU 600 as the data size (2 x 600 / 8 = 150) and forgetting the 20-byte header of each fragment.
Answering 72 or 216: giving the offset of the second or the fourth fragment. The first fragment has offset 0, so the third has 2 x 72, not 1 x 72 or 3 x 72.

recognize.clues: An MTU smaller than the packet, a fixed 20-byte header in every fragment, and a question about the fragment offset value of a numbered fragment.
recognize.contrast: The IP header topic lists the offset field, but sizing the fragments and counting offsets in 8-byte units is fragmentation; do not confuse it with the total length or header length fields.

check.body: Test the answer against the offset unit instead of the splitting. An offset of 144 units means 144 x 8 = 1152 data bytes precede the third fragment. Two full fragments of 576 bytes give 2 x 576 = 1152, so the offsets agree. Each of those fragments is 576 + 20 = 596 bytes, within the 600-byte MTU, while the next multiple of 8, 584, would need 604 bytes and overflow it.

questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the routing protocols, Routing Information Protocol (RIP) and Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) in an IPv4 network. I: RIP uses distance vector routing II: RIP packets are sent using UDP III: OSPF packets are sent using TCP IV: OSPF operation is based on link-state routing. Which of the statements above are CORRECT?

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: Distance vector routing: each router sends its table of distances to its neighbours and updates with the Bellman-Ford rule. Link-state routing: each router floods the state of its own links to all routers, then every router computes shortest paths on the same map with Dijkstra's algorithm. RIP is the standard distance vector protocol and OSPF is the standard link-state protocol. TCP and UDP are transport protocols. UDP is connectionless and simple; TCP is reliable and connection oriented. The rule: know which family each protocol belongs to and how its messages travel.

steps.title: Check each statement
steps.body: I: RIP is a distance vector protocol, so I is true. II: RIP messages are carried in UDP datagrams on port 520, so II is true. III: OSPF does not use TCP or UDP; its messages ride directly in IP datagrams (IP protocol number 89), and OSPF has its own acknowledgements for its link-state updates, so III is false. IV: OSPF is based on link-state routing, so IV is true.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: The correct statements are I, II and IV: option (C).

shortcut.body: RIP = distance vector over UDP; OSPF = link state, directly over IP (no TCP). So I, II, IV. 20 seconds.

traps.text: Option A leaves out II. RIP does use UDP (port 520), so a statement that is true was dropped.
Option B accepts III and drops IV. OSPF does not use TCP, and it is link state.
Option D drops I and accepts III. RIP is distance vector, and OSPF packets do not use TCP.

recognize.clues: Four statements name RIP and OSPF and ask which routing family each belongs to and which transport carries it.
recognize.contrast: Both are interior gateway protocols, so the family is the distinguishing feature: RIP exchanges distance tables with neighbours, OSPF floods link states and runs a shortest path computation.

check.body: Check by elimination on the transport statements. If III were true the OSPF messages would need a TCP connection per neighbour, but OSPF floods updates to a multicast group, which TCP cannot do. That settles III as false, and the only option listing I, II and IV without III remains.

questions.stem: The maximum number of IPv4 router addresses that can be listed in the record route (RR) option field of an IPv4 header is ______.

solutionDiagram.alt: An IPv4 header of 60 bytes: 20 fixed bytes then a 40-byte options field. Inside the options field the Record Route option uses 3 bytes for type, length and pointer, then nine 4-byte address slots A1 to A9, then one byte of padding.

steps.title: Terms and the rule
steps.body: The IPv4 header has a fixed part of 20 bytes and an optional part called options. The header length field (HLEN) is 4 bits and counts 4-byte words, so its maximum is 15 words = 60 bytes. Hence the options area holds at most 60 - 20 = 40 bytes. The Record Route (RR) option asks every router on the path to write its own 4-byte IPv4 address into the packet. The option starts with 3 bytes: a type byte, a length byte and a pointer byte that shows where the next address goes. The rule: addresses = floor((40 - 3) / 4).

steps.title: Space in the options area
steps.body: The header can be at most 15 x 4 = 60 bytes and the fixed part uses 20, so options can use 40 bytes.

steps.title: Count the addresses
steps.body: RR uses 3 bytes for its type, length and pointer, leaving 40 - 3 = 37 bytes. Each address is 4 bytes, so floor(37 / 4) = 9 addresses fit, using 36 bytes. The 40-byte field is then 3 + 36 = 39 bytes used and 1 byte of padding. Answer: 9.

shortcut.body: Options area = 40 bytes. Minus the 3-byte option header = 37. Divide by 4 and round down: 9. 1 minute.

traps.text: Answering 10: dividing 40 by 4 and forgetting the 3 bytes the RR option needs for type, length and pointer.
Answering 15: confusing the maximum header length in words (15) with the number of addresses. The header is 60 bytes and 20 are fixed.
Answering 9.25: not rounding down. Only whole 4-byte addresses fit, so the answer is the floor.

recognize.clues: The words "record route option field of an IPv4 header" ask for a capacity that is limited by the maximum header length.
recognize.contrast: Fragmentation also reads header fields, but it works with the total length and offset; the capacity of options is fixed by the header length field alone.

check.body: Test the neighbouring counts. Ten addresses would need 3 + 40 = 43 bytes, which exceeds the 40-byte options area, so ten cannot fit. Nine addresses need 3 + 36 = 39 bytes, which fits with one byte spare.

hints.text: Where in the IPv4 header can extra information be stored, and how big can that area ever be? Start from the header length field.
The header length field has 4 bits and counts in units of 4 bytes. That caps the whole header, and the fixed part takes a known share of it.
An option is not only its payload. Each option begins with a few bytes of bookkeeping, and the payload that remains is filled with whole 4-byte addresses, so a partial address does not count.
Compute the room left for options, subtract the bytes the Record Route option uses before its first address, and divide what is left by the size of one address.

variation.stem: An IPv4 header carries a header length (HLEN) field of 12. The header holds no options other than a Record Route option, which uses 3 bytes for its type, length and pointer and then stores 4-byte router addresses. What is the maximum number of router addresses that can be recorded?
variation.explanation: The header is 12 x 4 = 48 bytes, of which 20 are fixed, leaving 28 bytes for options. After the 3 option bytes there are 25 bytes, and floor(25 / 4) = 6 whole addresses fit.
